Growth has been faster in recent years. Migration and longer life expectancy both played a part.
The population is very unequally distributed: England is about 84%, Wales around 5%, Scotland just over 8% and Northern Ireland less than 3%.

An ageing population: people are living longer than ever thanks to better living standards and health care. There is a record number of people aged 85 and over, which affects the cost of pensions and health care.
England 84 percent, Scotland just over 8 percent, Wales around 5 percent, Northern Ireland less than 3 percent

The population is ethnically diverse and changing rapidly, especially in large cities such as London. The most common description chosen in surveys is white (which includes people of European, Australian, Canadian, New Zealand and American descent). Other significant groups are people of Asian, black and mixed descent.

By law, men and women must not be discriminated against because of their gender or because they are, or are not, married. They have equal rights to work, own property, marry and divorce. Married parents are equally responsible for their children.
Women make up about half of the workforce. On average girls leave school with better qualifications than boys, and more women than men study at university.
Women work in all sectors, with more in high-level positions than ever. Men now work in more varied jobs too.
Women often keep working after having children; in many families both partners work and share childcare and chores.

Religion and patron saints · Life in the UK
The UK is historically a Christian country. Everyone has the legal right to choose their religion, or to choose not to practise one.
There are religious buildings for other religions all over the UK: Islamic mosques, Hindu temples, Jewish synagogues, Sikh gurdwaras and Buddhist temples.

Called the Anglican Church in other countries and the Episcopal Church in Scotland and the USA. Protestant; has existed since the Reformation in the 1530s. The monarch is its head; the Archbishop of Canterbury is its spiritual leader. The monarch can select the Archbishop and senior officials, but usually the Prime Minister and a Church committee choose. Several bishops sit in the House of Lords.
A Presbyterian Church governed by ministers and elders. The chairperson of its General Assembly is the Moderator, appointed for one year only, who often speaks for the Church.
There is no established Church in Wales or Northern Ireland.
Other Protestant groups: Baptists, Methodists, Presbyterians and Quakers. The biggest other denomination is Roman Catholic.
